newsitem.title: UK: OFTEL optimistic on prospects for UK digital TV.
newsitem.headline: OFTEL optimistic on prospects for UK digital TV.

text.p: Good progress has been made in recent months towards the launch of multi-channel digital television in Britain, OFTEL Director General Don Cruickshank said on Wednesday.
"We have seen a deal more progress than I think many would have guessed," Cruickshank told reporters at a briefing.
"There are distinct prospects of UK consumers getting world class services very quickly indeed," he added.
Watchdog OFTEL is responsible for regulating conditional access, the means of ensuring pay television services are received only by those who have paid for them.

Pay television giant British Sky Broadcasting Plc said it plans to launch digital satellite with up to 200 channels by the end of this year. Cable companies are also gearing up to go digital this year while a 30-channel terrestrial version is expected to be launched in mid-1998.
Consumers will need new set-top boxes to receive the digital services, irrespective of the delivery method.
Publishing modified guidelines on conditional access, Cruickshank said he was writing to all companies involved for details of their negotiations on planned services.

"I shall be writing formally to all interested parties asking them to let me have within the next two weeks a record of their discussions to date and a clear indication of how they intend to meet their obligations," Cruickshank said.

He said the information would cover proposals on pricing, subscriber management and authorisation, electronic programme guides and the way in which satellite programmes are supplied to cable companies.
Some in the media industry have voiced fears that BSkyB's expertise in subscriber management will enable it to gain a stranglehold on conditional access, the so-called "gateway" to digital services.
But OFTEL has said it will ensure fair terms for all.
Cruickshank said there were few major changes to draft guidelines he published in December.
But he said that the rules on electronic programme guides, vital to navigate around a sea of channels, had been reviewed.
Guidelines will cover the order in which programmes are listed, the use of branding and the ease of purchasing pay-per-view options.
